title: The eclipse that did not test relativity
summary: On 21 August 1914 a total eclipse crossed the Crimea. Erwin Freundlich's Berlin expedition had gone there to measure whether starlight bends round the Sun, as Einstein predicted — and was interned as enemy aliens when Germany and Russia went to war three weeks before totality.
body: Einstein's 1911 prediction (half the value general relativity would give in 1915) could have been tested — and 'disproved' — that August. War spared the theory an embarrassment and delayed its test until Eddington's expedition of May 1919, which made Einstein famous months after Versailles.[^pais-1982] Freundlich and his instruments were held in Russia and exchanged for Russian officers in September 1914.[^crelinsten-2006] Meanwhile in Berlin, Einstein spent the autumn of 1914 on the flawed 'Entwurf' theory, the last detour before the field equations of November 1915.[^pais-1982]

the test that finally happened — and made relativity a world story

title: Moseley joins the Royal Engineers
summary: Henry Moseley, twenty-six, had just shown that the atomic number — not the atomic weight — orders the elements, from the X-ray spectra of the metals. In August 1914 he left Rutherford's laboratory and the Manchester–Oxford circle to take a commission as a signals officer. He was killed at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915.
body: Moseley's law (1913) turned Mendeleev's table from an empirical arrangement into a count of nuclear charge, predicted the missing elements (43, 61, 72, 75), and tied chemistry to Rutherford's nucleus and Bohr's atom.[^heilbron-1974] His death at Suvla Bay is the case usually cited when the war's cost to science is counted; after 1915 Britain kept more of its scientists out of the line.[^heilbron-1974] The card stands for the others who enlisted in August 1914 — among them Lawrence Bragg and the young Göttingen and Cambridge physicists — and for the question of what a year of silence in the laboratories cost.

title: The Manifesto of the Ninety-Three — and Einstein's reply
summary: On 4 October 1914 ninety-three German scholars and artists — Planck, Röntgen, Haber, Ostwald, Klein among the scientists — published 'An die Kulturwelt!', denying German war guilt and the Belgian atrocities and defending the army as the guardian of German culture. Einstein was one of four who signed a counter-manifesto 'to the Europeans' calling for a united Europe; it circulated privately and changed nothing.
body: The Manifesto did more damage to German science abroad than any defeat: it made the international scientific community a casualty of the war, and German scientists were excluded from international bodies until the mid-1920s.[^ungern-sternberg-1996] Several signatories later said they had signed without reading it; Planck distanced himself publicly in 1916.[^ungern-sternberg-1996] Einstein's 'Aufruf an die Europäer', drafted by Georg Friedrich Nicolai, gathered four signatures and was not published until 1917 — a first sign of the pacifist public figure he became.[^pais-1982]
